linear-inequalities.alt: Number line showing the solution x < −2 to the inequality 3 − 2x > 7, with an open circle at −2 and shading to the left, and the steps showing the sign flip.
linear-inequalities.figAlt: Four number lines showing x less than 1 (open circle, shade left), x less than or equal to 1 (closed circle, shade left), x greater than 1 (open circle, shade right), and x greater than or equal to 1 (closed circle, shade right).
linear-inequalities.caption: Strict inequalities use an open circle; inequalities that include equality use a closed circle.

exponents-and-equivalent-expressions.alt: Cheat sheet of six exponent rules: product, power of a power, quotient, zero exponent, negative exponent, and fractional exponent.
exponents-and-equivalent-expressions.figAlt: Worked example (2x³)² = 4x⁶, contrasted with the wrong answer 2x⁶ that forgets to square the coefficient.
exponents-and-equivalent-expressions.caption: An exponent outside parentheses applies to the coefficient as well as the variable.

ratios-rates-and-units.alt: Conversion chain turning 90 kilometers per hour into 25 meters per second by multiplying by 1000 meters per kilometer and 1 hour per 3600 seconds, with units cancelling.
ratios-rates-and-units.figAlt: A bar split 3 to 5 representing 40 total: the 3 parts equal 15 and the 5 parts equal 25, showing that the ratio 3 to 5 has 8 parts in all.
ratios-rates-and-units.caption: Add the ratio parts to get the whole, then divide to find the size of one part.

one-variable-data.alt: Bar chart of the data set 3, 5, 6, 8 and 28 with the median 6 and the mean 10 marked, showing the outlier 28 pulls the mean above the median.
one-variable-data.figAlt: Steps for finding a missing value: five numbers have a mean of 12 so the total is 60; four known numbers sum to 48, so the fifth number is 12.
one-variable-data.caption: Turn the mean into a total, subtract what you know, and what is left is the missing value.

right-triangles-and-trigonometry.alt: Right triangle with sides 3, 4 and 5 and angle A opposite the side of length 3, giving sin A = 3/5, cos A = 4/5 and tan A = 3/4.
right-triangles-and-trigonometry.figAlt: The same 3-4-5 triangle with angles A and B, showing that the sine of one acute angle equals the cosine of the other, both 3/5.
right-triangles-and-trigonometry.caption: The two acute angles add to 90°, so the side opposite one is adjacent to the other.

area-and-volume.alt: A square of side 3 and a square of side 6 showing the area grows from 9 to 36, a factor of 4, while a cube's volume grows from 27 to 216, a factor of 8.
area-and-volume.figAlt: Grid of formulas: rectangle area, triangle area, circle area, rectangular prism volume, cylinder volume, and sphere volume.
area-and-volume.caption: Most of these are on the SAT reference sheet, so practice reading them, not memorizing them.

nonlinear-functions.alt: Graph of f(x) = 100(1.2)^x rising and g(x) = 100(0.8)^x falling, both starting at 100 when x is 0.
nonlinear-functions.figAlt: The form f(x) = a times b to the x, with a as the starting value and b as the growth factor, noting that 20 percent growth means b is 1.20, not 0.20.
nonlinear-functions.caption: Convert the percent to a multiplier before writing the equation.

rhetorical-synthesis.alt: Diagram of a rhetorical synthesis question: a bulleted list of student notes flows through a stated goal to the one answer choice that uses the right notes.
rhetorical-synthesis.figAlt: Three-step method for rhetorical synthesis: find the goal, match the notes it needs, and reject choices that miss the goal or add facts not in the notes.
rhetorical-synthesis.caption: A correct choice meets the goal using only the notes provided.

central-ideas-and-details.alt: Tree diagram with the main idea at the top supported by three detail boxes beneath it.
central-ideas-and-details.figAlt: Three-part scale: a choice that only covers one detail is too narrow, one that covers the whole passage is just right, and one that claims more than the passage says is too broad.
central-ideas-and-details.caption: Wrong choices usually fail by being too narrow or going beyond the text.
